paras: The Wahalak race riot was an armed clash near Wahalak, Kemper County, Mississippi, on December 16, 1888, in which Black men at the home of a Black man named Maury fired on a white posse, followed by a white manhunt in which Black homes were burned. Between two and five white men were reported killed, among them Constable Seth Cobb and Henry Maury. Three Black captives were later said by their guards to have "escaped," and other Black men were reported shot or hanged, reports that Meridian dispatches denied.

Meridian men back from the scene said the trouble began when a Black man whose wagon collided with that of G. F. Nicholson's son knocked the elder Nicholson senseless with a pistol. A Columbus account instead described a boys' fight and a beating of Constable Cobb as he served a warrant, and a West Point dispatch traced it to a gin-house fire. The Meridian account added that two unnamed white men had organized about ten Black men at a church to resist Maury's arrest.

That Sunday night the posse found Maury's house empty and was fired on in three volleys from the cotton house, which killed Henry Maury and Cobb and wounded William Vaughan, J. F. Maury and John Dew. Columbus and Macon reports put the posse at twelve and the attackers at about fifty, with five whites killed. Meridian said "not a single negro" was known to be hurt, though prisoners later reportedly named George Maury, Cash Maury and George Coleman as wounded.

On December 17 fifty white men found the place deserted and burned its buildings and those of an adjoining farm, and a Meridian dispatch said all the accused men's stock was killed. On December 19 searchers arrested Dick Cheatham and Anthony Wilder and held them at the "White House," an empty building; a Picayune dispatch said "their fate will be determined in twenty-four hours." The same day a Wahalak dispatch reported that a posse had overtaken four of the accused, shot one and hanged three, and a Black man, Pompey Coleman, reported Cash Maury and Allen Coleman killed. On December 20 the guards said Cheatham, Wilder and Zach Maury had got away and asked that their names be struck from the list of sixteen. A Meridian dispatch of December 21 said the bodies of "Maury, Coleman and Davis" were hanging from a pine tree near Wahalak.

The searchers disbanded on December 20 with thirteen men at large; three more unnamed men were reported captured by December 25. Two newspaper correspondents were reported ordered out of Kemper County because of the tone of their articles. Governor Lowry had no official word by December 18, and a report that troops were ordered out was called untrue. The Meridian account predicted no proceedings against the whites, and no report of an inquest or trial for any Black death appears in the coverage.

The first wires varied wildly: the Evening World counted nine whites dead, while the New Orleans States reported "twelve white men and one hundred and fifty negroes" dead. By December 19 the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer called those reports "gross exaggerations," and the Emporia Weekly News headed the Meridian story "Massacre Modified."

Headlines spoke of a "race war" and "negro murderers," and the Richmond Daily Times headed the hanging report "The Negro Participants to be Exterminated." The Memphis Appeal's correspondent blamed "the educated negro" Walter Crook and called the guards "grim humorists," while the South Kentuckian put "escaped" in quotation marks. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union doubted that state officials would "hold the scales evenly," and the St. Paul Western Appeal cited "the outrage at Wehalak" in an editorial titled "The Bloody South." The New-York Tribune printed a claim by Dr. H. Clay Chisolm that the white Maury brothers had been Kemper County Ku Klux.

Later reports from the scene named only Cobb and Henry Maury as killed, against five in the Macon list, and the Memphis Appeal's claim that little property was destroyed conflicts with the Meridian reports. Black deaths were never confirmed: Meridian called the rumors "utterly without foundation," the Waterbury dispatch called its own news untrustworthy, and Cash Maury, reported killed, was later listed as wounded.

reader.title: Wahalak race riot
bases: After Black men fired on a white posse, armed whites burned the Maury place, adjoining cabins and stock and hunted sixteen named Black men, three of whom vanished from the posse's guard and others of whom were reported shot or hanged (A4, A7, A21, A13).

The ambush, the white deaths, the burning and the capture of three men are corroborated by independent Meridian, Macon, Columbus and Memphis reports (A4, A15, A7, A21), but the killing of Black men is reported (A13, A22) and denied (A12) in the coverage.

accounts.label: Meridian posse's account
accounts.gist: A wagon collision led to an assault on Nicholson; two white men organized Black men to resist Maury's arrest; the posse was fired on in three volleys from the cotton house, losing Henry Maury and Cobb, and no Black man was known hurt.

accounts.label: Columbus and Macon specials
accounts.gist: A fight between a Black boy and a white boy led to a warrant; Constable Cobb was beaten serving it; his posse of twelve was ambushed by about fifty Black men, five killed and six wounded.

accounts.label: Picayune West Point special
accounts.gist: A Black man suspected of burning a gin-house beat an officer and escaped; the posse sent after him was ambushed, four killed and eight wounded.

accounts.label: Wahalak dispatches of Dec 19
accounts.gist: A posse overtook four of the accused, shot one and hanged three; Pompey Coleman reported Cash Maury and Allen Coleman killed.

accounts.label: Meridian denials
accounts.gist: The rumor that several Black men were killed near Wahalak was 'utterly without foundation'.

accounts.label: Memphis Appeal staff correspondent
accounts.gist: Three captives were reported by their guards to have got away and were 'doubtless' put out of harm's way; thirteen fled; little property destroyed.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal blamed an 'educated negro', Sherman and Northern letters, praised the whites' 'unusual moderation', and called the guards 'grim humorists'.
The Richmond Daily Times headed the hanging report 'The Negro Participants to be Exterminated'; the Wahpeton Times ran 'The Avengers at Work'.
Most papers ran the wires under 'race war' headlines with 'negro murderers' and 'assassins', some noting the first reports were exaggerated.
The Sacramento Daily Record-Union feared a 'local war of races' and doubted the state would 'hold the scales evenly'.
The Western Appeal of St. Paul called it 'the outrage at Wehalak' in an editorial on post-election lynchings, 'The Bloody South'.

conflicts.note: The later Meridian and Memphis Appeal reports from the scene, which name the burials of Cobb and Maury, are the better evidence for two; the five-name list includes men others report as wounded.

record_check.dossier: The ambush was Sunday night, December 16; the burning was December 17; captures and reported hangings December 18-20.

record_check.record: 36 names including Seth Cobb, Henry Maury, Vaughan, Hare, Nicholson, Harpers, Giles, Dew, Jeff Thomas
record_check.dossier: The list mixes the white posse's dead and wounded (Cobb, Henry and J. F. Maury, Vaughan, Hare, Nicholson, Dew/Drew/Dow, Giles, the Harpers, Frank Maury, Jeff Thomas) with the Black accused; the Black victims of the white response are Cheatham, Wilder, Zach Maury (captives who vanished), Cash Maury and Allen Coleman (reported killed) and 'Maury, Coleman and Davis' (reported hanged).
Contested: 0 per Meridian, 2-4 per Wahalak dispatches, 3 hanged per one Meridian dispatch, plus three captives missing.
Two (Cobb, Henry Maury) per later reports; five per Macon list; four, nine or twelve in first wires.
At least two white deaths are firm; Black deaths are contested.
Three (George Maury, Cash Maury, George Coleman) per prisoners' statements; none known per Meridian.
The three captives were held by the searchers' own guards, not by officers, and were reported to have 'escaped'; the four reportedly hanged were 'overtaken' in pursuit.
Armed white men of Kemper and adjoining counties and railroad towns, organized under unnamed 'captains'; no individual named.

record_check.record: friends of the whites were shot by colored men at Wahalak
record_check.dossier: Supported: revenge for the posse members killed in the ambush.

info: Ambush of the white posse on Sunday night, December 16, 1888; manhunt December 17-20; reported hangings and disappearance of captives December 18-20.
House of a Black man named Maury, about seven miles from Wahalak, a village on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad (also printed Walhalla, Wahala, Polatka).

Black victims of the white response: Dick Cheatham, Anthony Wilder and Zach Maury (captured, then reported 'escaped'); Cash Maury and Allen Coleman (reported killed); 'Maury, Coleman and Davis' (reported hanged); four unnamed men (reported shot or hanged); the Maury place and nearby cabins burned and stock killed.
Accused of firing on the white posse from ambush at Maury's house; the original warrant was for a Black man accused of beating a white man (Nicholson) or, in one version, of burning a gin-house.
Armed white men of Kemper and neighboring counties, joined by parties from Meridian, Macon and other railroad towns; described as a posse and as 'avengers'.
Contested: none (Meridian, Dec 18-19), two or more (Wahalak, Dec 19), four (one shot, three hanged), three hanged (Maury, Coleman, Davis), and three captives 'got away' from their guards.
Search parties disbanded Dec 20 with thirteen of sixteen listed men at large; the three captives reported 'escaped' and their names struck from the list.
